title: Determining a Keyboard Activation Key as a Membership Test
reading_goal: The membership test checks whether keyboard input matches a set of permitted activation keys.
code:
activation_keys = {"Enter", " "}
pressed = "Enter"
should_activate = pressed in activation_keys
print(should_activate)
question: What does “`pressed in activation_keys`” being True mean from the perspective of UI behavior?
choices: This means that the key has been enabled as a keyboard target.
This means a mouse click occurred.
This means the focus was automatically lost.
It means every key has the same function.
answer: This means that the key has been enabled as a keyboard target.
explanation: 1) `activation_keys` contains `Enter` and `Space`. 2) `pressed` is `Enter`. 3) The membership test checks whether `Enter` is in the allowed set. 4) The result True is stored in `should_activate`.
project_context: It is used to read Enter/Space activation rules at the code level when implementing or testing keyboard accessibility.
reading_goal_internal: membership test가 키보드 입력을 허용된 활성화 키 집합과 대조하는 역할을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: The `in` membership test returns a boolean value indicating whether the left-hand side value is an element of the right-hand side collection.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, check which keys are allowed in the set on the right, and then verify whether the value of `pressed` is included in that set.
concept_explanation.key_point: The True/False result is directly linked to the accessibility rule that asks, “Should this key press be interpreted as an activation?”
concept_explanation.common_mistake: Do not interpret `True` as “the button has already been clicked.” This expression merely determines whether the button is active; the actual UI behavior is separate.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since `Escape` is not in the set of allowed characters, the membership test returns `False`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) `activation_keys` contains `Enter` and `Space`. 2) `pressed` is `Enter`. 3) The membership test checks whether `Enter` is in the allowed set. 4) The result True is stored in `should_activate`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: The True/False result is directly linked to the accessibility rule that asks, “Should this key press be interpreted as an activation?”

common_wrong_choice.choice: This means a mouse click occurred.
common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The code does not handle mouse events; it only checks whether the current key is a valid key.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Distinguish between evaluation results and actual event execution.

answer_explanation.takeaway: In the accessibility rules, ``in`` asks **whether the current input belongs to the set of allowed inputs**.

title: Read a focus-state comparison that makes the keyboard focus position visible.
reading_goal: Read not only the True/False results of the comparison, but also how they relate to the accessibility goal of visually indicating the keyboard focus position.
question: What is the UX purpose of linking the result of `focus_source == "keyboard"` to `show_focus_ring`?
choices: To enable keyboard users to visually identify the current focus position, turn on the focus indicator to
To store the mouse pointer position as a string,
To ensure that string comparison results are always True,
answer: To enable keyboard users to visually identify the current focus position, turn on the focus indicator to
explanation: 1) It checks whether `focus_source` is the keyboard. 2) Since they match, the result is `True`. 3) `True` is stored in `show_focus_ring`. 4) This state is used to turn on the indicator so that keyboard users can see the current focus position.
project_context: This is used when implementing visual indication policies, such as a focus ring, to ensure that keyboard navigation users do not miss the currently selected UI element.
reading_goal_internal: focus_source가 keyboard인지 비교한 bool을 포커스 링 표시 상태로 연결해, 키보드 사용자가 현재 포커스 위치를 시각적으로 확인하게 하는 목적을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: The `==` comparison checks whether two values are equal and returns True or False.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: It reads that the current value of `focus_source` is compared to `keyboard`, and that the resulting boolean is stored in `show_focus_ring`, which determines whether the UI displays the focus indicator.
concept_explanation.key_point: The UX purpose of this comparison is to enable users navigating with a keyboard to visually identify which element currently has focus by enabling the focus indicator.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: If you simply conclude that the value is True because the strings are identical, you miss the point of the card’s accessibility objective. You must also read about why this `bool` is linked to the focus indicator state.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since the source is a mouse, it is not the same as a keyboard, so `visible` is `False`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) `focus_source` is `keyboard`. 2) The comparison `focus_source == "keyboard"` evaluates to True. 3) True is stored in `show_focus_ring`. 4) This state is used to enable the focus indicator so that users navigating with the keyboard can see the current focus position.
answer_explanation.why_correct: The purpose of `legacy` is not simply to provide a comparison result, but to understand the accessibility state that visually reveals the current focus position for keyboard users.

common_wrong_choice.choice: To ensure that string comparison results are always True,
common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: A comparison returns True only when two strings are identical, and what is important in this code is that this boolean value determines the focus policy.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Don’t stop at the comparison results; trace the UI meaning of the state variables where those results are stored.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The **focus-state** code follows the flow: **check input method → evaluate as boolean → display the user’s focus position on the keyboard**.

title: Reading the name accessible via the icon button metadata
reading_goal: Use subscription to read the value of the `aria_label` key from a dict containing UI metadata.
question: What is the string retrieved by `button["aria_label"]`?
explanation: Find the `aria_label` key in the `button` dictionary. Its value is `다음 카드`. A bracket lookup returns this value and stores it in `accessible_name`. This is because the string actually stored in the `aria_label` key is `다음 카드`. A common source of confusion: ▶ ▶ is the value of the `icon` key, but the key being queried here is `aria_label`. Point of confusion: Carefully verify the key name inside the square brackets. Even when UI metadata is represented as a dictionary, read the values for each key separately.
project_context: Even icon buttons without text should have accessible names provided within the UI context so that users of assistive technology can understand their meaning.
reading_goal_internal: UI metadata를 담은 dict에서 aria_label key의 value를 subscription으로 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A dictionary key lookup `data["key"]` retrieves the value associated with that key.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Find the `aria_label` key in the `button` dictionary and check the value to its right.
concept_explanation.key_point: Separate the accessibility concept of `aria-label` from Python syntax. In Python, this is a card that reads the string value of the ``aria_label`` key.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: Since the icon ▶ is visible on the screen, it’s easy to assume that the name for assistive technology is also ▶. The metadata contains a separate string: “`다음 카드`.”

teaching_example.walkthrough: The string `닫기` associated with the `aria_label` key is printed.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: Find the `aria_label` key in the `button dict`. Its value is `다음 카드`. A bracket lookup returns this value and stores it in `accessible_name`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the string actually stored in the `aria_label` key is `다음 카드`.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: ▶ is the value of the icon key, and the current lookup key is aria_label.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Check the exact key name inside the square brackets.

answer_explanation.takeaway: If UI metadata is also represented as a dict, read it by separating the values by key.

title: Check whether the UI element’s tag is `button`
reading_goal: It determines whether a button is native by comparing the result of a `dict` lookup with a string literal using equality, and returns a boolean value.
question: What is the final output?
explanation: element["tag"] returns ``button``. ``button == button`` is `True`. The result is stored in `is_native_button` because the two strings are identical. A common source of confusion: `button button` is the comparison string, and the result of the equality expression is a boolean. Point of Misunderstanding: Distinguish between the data types of the comparison values and the comparison result. The comparison does not evaluate the values themselves but determines their relationship as True or False.
project_context: The click action is implemented using a native button element instead of a div to preserve the default semantics and support keyboard navigation in an accessibility context.
reading_goal_internal: dict lookup 결과와 문자열 literal을 equality로 비교해 native button 여부를 bool로 판단한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `==` is an operator that compares whether two values are equal and returns a boolean.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, convert the result of the left-hand side `subscription` into an actual string, and then compare it to the string on the right.
concept_explanation.key_point: The accessibility benefit of the “native button” is the domain context, and the Python focus is on verifying that the tag value is exactly “button.”
concept_explanation.common_mistake: Since the text inside the `element` dictionary is ``다음``, it is easy to assume that it is being compared to that value. However, the comparison is made against the value of the `tag` key.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since `div` and `button` are different, `False` is printed.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: element["tag"] returns `button`. `button == button` is True. The result is stored in is_native_button.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the two strings are identical.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `button` is the string being compared, and the result of the equality expression is a boolean.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Distinguish between the data types of the comparison operands and the comparison result.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A comparison does not return a value itself, but rather determines the relationship between two values as True or False.

title: Selecting explanatory text based on assistive technology usage
reading_goal: Track which string value the boolean state in a conditional expression selects.
code:
sr_text = "정답 선택 결과"
screen_reader_enabled = True
spoken_text = sr_text if screen_reader_enabled else ""
print(spoken_text)
question: `screen_reader_enabled` What is the final output when ``True``?
explanation: sr_text is “`정답 선택 결과`.” screen_reader_enabled is True. Therefore, the conditional expression selects sr_text before “if,” and that string is stored in spoken_text. This is because, under a True condition, the current value of the first candidate—sr_text—is selected. Common Misconception: “True True” is the conditional value that determines the selection, not a candidate stored in `spoken_text`. Point of Misinterpretation: Readers tend to separate the condition from the two values being selected. The conditional expression selects one of the two candidates based on the boolean state.
project_context: This is a card that uses Python value selection to convey accessibility UI context—which provides visual support for users of assistive devices—regarding state descriptions that lack visual cues.
reading_goal_internal: 조건 표현식에서 bool 상태가 어느 문자열 값을 선택하게 하는지 추적한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: The conditional expression `A if condition else B` selects A if `condition` is true and B if it is false.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, check the condition value in the middle, then read the actual variable value on the selected side.
concept_explanation.key_point: When the condition is True, what is selected is not the variable name `sr_text` itself, but the string that `sr_text` currently points to.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that the value "True" for `screen_reader_enabled` is included as-is in `spoken_text`. However, "True" is a selection criterion, and the candidate values are `sr_text` and an empty string.

teaching_example.code:
hint = "입력값을 확인하세요"
show_hint = False
message = hint if show_hint else ""
print(message)
teaching_example.walkthrough: Since the condition is False, an empty string is selected.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: sr_text is the `정답 선택 결과`. screen_reader_enabled is True. Therefore, the conditional expression selects sr_text before the if statement, and that string is stored in spoken_text.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Because with a True condition, the current value of `sr_text`, the candidate before the condition, is selected.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `True` is a conditional value that determines the selection; it is not a candidate stored in `spoken_text`.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Read the condition and the positions of the two selected values separately.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A conditional expression selects one actual value from two candidates based on a boolean condition.

title: Reading text color values from the `theme` dictionary
reading_goal: Use a `dict` subscription to accurately read specific key values from the accessibility theme settings.
question: What value does `theme["text"]` return?
explanation: The `theme` dictionary contains `text:#111` and `background:#fff`. Since `focus` looks up the `text` key, it returns `#111`. This is because a dictionary lookup returns the value associated with the key enclosed in square brackets. A common source of confusion: #fff #fff is the value of the `background` key. The key being looked up is `text`. Point of confusion: This occurs when different key-value pairs in the dictionary are misinterpreted. A dictionary lookup finds the exact value based on the key inside the square brackets.
project_context: In the learning app, this is linked to code that reads theme values—such as text and background colors—from the configuration data, which affect accessibility.
reading_goal_internal: dict subscription으로 접근성 theme 설정의 특정 key 값을 정확히 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: In a `dict`, ``mapping[key]`` is a subscription expression that reads the value associated with the given key.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, check the key inside the square brackets, then find the exact same key in the dict and retrieve the associated value.
concept_explanation.key_point: UI policies, such as color contrast, can also be expressed as Python configuration dictionaries, and when reading the code, you first check which key’s value is being referenced.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to confuse the `text` and `background` values. You must first check what the `key` inside the square brackets actually is.

teaching_example.walkthrough: The subscription reads and outputs #eee, which is bound to the "panel" key.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: The `theme` dictionary contains `text:#111` and `background:#fff`. Since `focus` looks up the `text` key, it returns `#111`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because a `dict` subscription returns the value associated with the key enclosed in square brackets.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `#fff` is the value of the `background` key. The current lookup key is `text`.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an example of misreading different key-value pairs in a `dict`.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A dictionary lookup finds the exact value based on the key inside the square brackets.

title: skip link Storing information in a single dict
reading_goal: Read the flow in which the dict literal containing the destination and label of `skip-link` is evaluated and stored in the `skip_link` variable.
question: What is printed when you read `skip_link["href"]` after the assignment?
explanation: In the dict on the right side of the assignment, the `href` key links to `#main`. This dict is stored in `skip_link`, and looking up the same key returns `#main`. This is because the assigned dict preserves the key-value relationships exactly as they were. Common source of confusion: “Skip to main text.” That string is the value of the `text` key, but the question checks the `href` key. Point of misinterpretation: This occurs when the roles of the two fields within the dictionary are confused. When assigning complex data, track both the entire right-hand object and its internal key-value relationships together.
project_context: This connects to code that treats the destination and display text of a skip link, which lets keyboard users bypass repeated menus, as UI state data.
reading_goal_internal: skip-link의 목적지와 표시문을 담은 dict literal이 평가되어 skip_link 변수에 저장되는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: The `assignment` operator calculates the value on the right and stores it in the variable on the left. If the right-hand side is a dictionary literal, you can group multiple related fields into a single object.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: After checking each key and value inside the `dict`, we see which variable the entire object is stored in.
concept_explanation.key_point: Even when representing UI information using Python data rather than HTML itself, you can group the destination and the label within the same structure.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that `href` and `text` are created as separate variables. In reality, a single dictionary is stored in `skip_link`.

teaching_example.walkthrough: The entire dict with two fields is stored in `help_link`, and you can access the `href` value `#help` again.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: In the dict on the right side of `assignment`, the `href` key links to `#main`. This dict is stored in `skip_link`, and looking up the same key returns `#main`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the assigned dict preserves the key-value relationships exactly as they are.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: That string is the value of the `text` key, while the question looks up the `href` key.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an example of misinterpreting the roles of two fields within a `dict`.

answer_explanation.takeaway: When assigning composite data, track the entire object on the right along with its internal key-value relationships.

title: Selecting the reduced-motion duration using a conditional expression
reading_goal: Read how, depending on the condition in the conditional expression, one of the two candidates is selected and passed to the assignment.
code:
prefers_reduced_motion = True
duration_ms = 0.01 if prefers_reduced_motion else 300
print(duration_ms)
question: When `prefers_reduced_motion` is True, what is the value of `duration_ms`?
explanation: The condition is True. The conditional expression selects 0.01 before the `if` statement, and the assignment stores that value in `duration_ms`. This is because, when the condition is True, the first value in the conditional expression becomes the result. Common mistake: 300. 300 is the `else` value selected when the condition is `False`. Point of confusion: This occurs when the current Boolean value of the condition is interpreted incorrectly. The conditional expression evaluates the middle condition first and selects one result value.
project_context: This connects to an example that expresses accessibility behavior—which reduces non-essential transition times based on the settings of motion-sensitive users—as Python configuration logic.
reading_goal_internal: conditional expression의 조건값에 따라 두 후보 중 어느 값이 선택되어 assignment로 전달되는지 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `value_if_true if condition else value_if_false` is a conditional expression that selects one of two values based on the result of the condition.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Evaluate the middle condition first; select the left value when True and the value after `else` when False.
concept_explanation.key_point: When UI behavior changes according to user settings, a conditional expression can turn the selected outcome into a single value.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that 0.01 is always selected when reading the code from left to right. However, the condition in the middle determines which value to use first.

teaching_example.code:
compact = False
spacing = 4 if compact else 12
print(spacing)
teaching_example.walkthrough: Since `compact` is False, the value 12 from the `else` branch is stored in `spacing`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: The condition is True. The conditional expression selects 0.01 from the expression before the `if` statement, and the assignment stores that value in `duration_ms`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because, in the case of “True,” the first value in the conditional expression becomes the result.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: 300 is the value selected by the `else` clause when the condition is False.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where the current Boolean value of the condition is inverted.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A conditional expression evaluates the condition in the middle first and then selects one of the possible outcomes.

title: Check whether the target and input ID match using an `if` statement
reading_goal: Read the execution flow where the result of comparing the target string with the input ID determines the if/else branch.
question: What is the output when both identifiers are `search`?
explanation: Both variables point to the string `search`. The comparison ``==`` evaluates to `True`, so the `if` block executes and `linked` is printed. This is because the two strings in the `if` condition are exactly the same. A common source of confusion: `mismatch` is the output of the `else` branch, which runs when the comparison evaluates to `False`. Common Misinterpretation: This occurs when the comparison result is applied in reverse. An `if` statement evaluates the condition to a value and executes only one branch.
project_context: This relates to accessibility validation, specifically checking whether the target indicated by a label in a search bar or filter input matches the actual control ID.
reading_goal_internal: label 대상 문자열과 input id를 비교한 결과가 if/else 분기를 결정하는 실행 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: An `if` statement executes the body when the result of the conditional expression is `True`; if it is `False`, the associated `else` path is selected.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, check the current values of the two variables being compared, calculate the result using ``==``, and then proceed to the actual execution block.
concept_explanation.key_point: The accessibility context—that the same identifier is used when linking a form label to an input—can be expressed using a Python comparison flow.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that two strings are True if they look similar. ``==`` compares whether the actual string values are the same.

teaching_example.walkthrough: If the two strings are the same, the `if` condition evaluates to `True`, and “linked” is printed.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: Both variables refer to the string `search`. The `==` comparison becomes True, so the `if` body runs and `linked` is printed.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the two strings in the `if` expression are exactly the same.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `mismatch` is the output of the `else` branch that executes when the comparison evaluates to `False`.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an example of applying the comparison results in reverse.

answer_explanation.takeaway: An `if` statement evaluates the condition as an actual value and then executes only one branch.

title: Reading the `aria-live` setting from the accessibility attributes dictionary
reading_goal: Accurately retrieve the `aria-live` value from a dict containing accessibility attributes.
question: `live_mode` What value is stored here?
explanation: `region['aria-live']` looks up the `aria-live` key and returns its value, `polite`. This is because a dictionary subscription simply reads the value associated with the specified key. Commonly confused incorrect answer: This is the correct answer. That string is the value of the `text` key. Point of misinterpretation: This occurs when a different value from the same dictionary is selected without verifying the lookup key. In Python, accessibility settings also follow the pattern of **verifying the key → retrieving the corresponding value**.
project_context: This relates to the context of managing accessibility attributes so that assistive devices can convey changes to the user when the screen dynamically updates—such as when a learning app displays whether an answer is correct.
reading_goal_internal: 접근성 속성을 담은 dict에서 aria-live 값을 정확히 조회한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `mapping[key]` is a subscription that reads the value associated with a specific key in a dict.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, check the key inside the square brackets, then look up the value for that key in the dict.
concept_explanation.key_point: Here, the key aspect of Python syntax is retrieving the `aria-live` value, and `polite` is linked to the way dynamic changes are signaled in the accessibility UI.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to mistake the string in the `text` key for the query result. The actual query key is `aria-live`.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since the lookup key is “`aria-label`,” the result is “`닫기`.”

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `region['aria-live']` It looks up the key "`aria-live`" and returns its value, "`polite`."
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because a dictionary subscription reads the value of the specified key exactly as it is.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: That string is the value of the `text` key.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case of choosing another value from the same dict without checking the lookup key.

answer_explanation.takeaway: In Python, accessibility settings are also read as **check the key → look up the corresponding value**.

title: Reading the Tab Order Using a List Literal
reading_goal: Read the items in the list in the order that the keyboard focus moves through them.
question: What comes after ``Search`` in this list?
explanation: If you read the list items from left to right, the order is Header, Search, Card. Therefore, Card comes after Search. This is because Python lists preserve the order in which items are written. A common source of confusion: “Choices” is the item that follows “Card.” A potential misreading occurs when the list order is skipped by one position. For data where order is meaningful, **the positional relationships within the list are tracked exactly as they are**.
project_context: This relates to accessibility quality, specifically the design of the focus order so that learners using only a keyboard can navigate screen elements in a predictable sequence.
reading_goal_internal: 리스트의 항목 순서를 키보드 포커스 이동 순서와 연결해 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A list literal is a Python expression that contains multiple values in a specified order.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Read the values inside the square brackets from left to right and preserve the position of each item.
concept_explanation.key_point: Since the tab order itself is meaningful, a change in the order of list items can be interpreted as a change in the user’s navigation sequence.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to read a list like an unordered set. A list preserves item order.

teaching_example.walkthrough: If you represent the keyboard navigation sequence as data, you can read it in the order: Menu, then Form, and finally Submit.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: When reading the list items from left to right, the order is Header, Search, and Card. Therefore, Card comes after Search.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because Python lists preserve the order in which items are written.

common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where the list elements are skipped by one position.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Data where order is meaningful **tracks the positional relationships within the list exactly as they are**.

title: Reading the `if` statement that executes a focus trap when a modal opens
reading_goal: Read the sequence in which the boolean state determines whether the focus-trap call in the if block is executed.
code:
modal_open = True
modal = "help"
events = []

def keep_focus_inside(name):
    events.append(name)

if modal_open:
    keep_focus_inside(modal)
question: What is the direct reason why `keep_focus_inside(modal)` is executed in this code?
explanation: Since `modal_open` is True, the if condition is true. Therefore, the indented call to `keep_focus_inside(modal)` is executed. This is because the body of an if statement is executed when the condition is truthy. A common source of confusion: Just because a function is defined does not mean it is automatically called by the definition alone. Point of misinterpretation: This occurs when the function definition and the conditional call are not distinguished. Conditional UI behavior should be read in the following order: **check state value → if condition → determine whether to call the body**.
project_context: This relates to an accessibility implementation that prevents keyboard focus from shifting to the background UI while the modal is open.
reading_goal_internal: boolean 상태가 if 본문의 focus-trap 호출 실행 여부를 결정하는 순서를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `if condition:` The indented body is executed only when the condition is truthy.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: After checking the current value of the conditional variable, it determines whether to execute the body or skip it.
concept_explanation.key_point: Separate from the UI purpose of a focus trap, the Python rule is that the truth value of `modal_open` determines whether the call occurs.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: Since the function is written below the `if` statement, it’s easy to assume it always executes. However, it is not called if the condition is `False`.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since `panel_open` is False, the body of the `if` statement is not executed.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: Since `modal_open` is True, the if condition is true. Therefore, the indented call to `keep_focus_inside(modal)` is executed.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: A function call does not execute automatically just by defining the function.

title: Compare whether the `aria-describedby` reference matches the error ID

Common wrong answer: `error1`. `error1` is a value used in the comparison; the comparison expression itself produces a boolean. title: Check the accessibility structure using the card title link metadata

answer: Ensuring that the structure of the card’s title and body is understandable even to assistive technologies

This is because accessibility encompasses not only the visual layout on the screen but also a structure that allows assistive technologies to interpret relationships. Common misconception: Contrary to the belief that hiding validation results is a form of accessibility suppression, accessibility structure actually makes information accessible to a wider audience. Point of confusion: This arises from confusing “accessibility” with “visibility suppression.” An accessibility component checks whether **the relationship between a semantic element and its label is actually established**.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Accessibility structures do not hide information; rather, they make it understandable to a wider audience.

title: View “accessibility” as a product quality requirement
reading_goal: Read the structure where product quality is evaluated as "True" only when both accessibility and wider user usability are satisfied.
code:
quality = {"accessibility": True, "usable_by_more_people": True}
is_product_quality = quality["accessibility"] and quality["usable_by_more_people"]
question: Why should accessibility be considered a measure of product quality?
choices: To enable more users to learn reliably,
answer: To enable more users to learn reliably,
explanation: Since both conditions—accessibility and usable_by_more_people—are True, the product-quality judgment is also True. This is because improving accessibility is directly linked to actual usability for a broader user base. A common source of confusion: To delete all cards, accessibility quality and data deletion are unrelated. Point of Misinterpretation: This occurs when the concept of product quality is confused with a destructive operation. a11y is interpreted as a quality issue concerning **who can actually use the product**.
project_context: In a learning app with over 1,000 screens, this stage is linked not only to the number of features but also to ensuring the UI quality that allows more users to use the app reliably.
reading_goal_internal: 접근성과 더 많은 사용자 사용 가능성을 함께 만족해야 product quality 판단이 True가 되는 구조를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check the value of each quality flag individually and then calculate the result.
concept_explanation.key_point: Accessibility should be viewed not as a mere add-on, but as a quality attribute that enables more users to use the product reliably.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to think of accessibility as a separate feature intended only for a specific minority of users.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Accessibility quality and data deletion are unrelated.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case of confusing a product-quality concept with a destructive operation.
